title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day
hook: remembered each year, he is often called the shield of India

segments.voice: Yesterday, shaheed, and two small boys at Sirhind who would not bend. Your line was small, and unbending. Today, another martyr, and a shelter for strangers.

Strangers arrive at your door. They aren't your people, and they don't share your faith. They've traveled a long way, and they're frightened. Our families are being pressured to give up our religion, they say, and we don't know who else to ask. What would you say? Sikhs remember that this is what happened at Anandpur in 1675. The visitors were Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars and priests. The man they came to see was the ninth Guru.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE DOOR.` → `NOT YOUR FAITH, NOT YOUR PEOPLE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU SAY?`

segments.voice: Guru Tegh Bahadur listened. Tradition says he sat quiet a long time, then said it would take the sacrifice of a great soul. His son Gobind, about nine years old, answered: who could be greater than you? So the Guru sent the Pandits back with a message for the officials of the emperor Aurangzeb: if Tegh Bahadur can be made to change his faith, we will all change ours. Then he set out for Delhi himself. He was arrested. Three of his companions, Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, were put to death in front of him, tradition says, to break him. He didn't break. In November 1675, in the square at Chandni Chowk in Delhi, he was beheaded. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands on the spot now. Sikhs hold on to this: he gave his life for other people's right to worship, a right he didn't need for himself. He didn't wear their sacred thread or their forehead mark. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, later wrote that his father protected their tilak and their thread, and gave his head but not his faith. So he is called Hind di Chadar. Hind is India. A chadar is a sheet, a covering, the cloth you'd put over someone to shelter them. The covering of India. His own verses in the Guru Granth Sahib say, in paraphrase, that the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one. Sikhs mark his martyrdom every year, in late autumn, with kirtan, and many visit Sis Ganj.
screen: `A PLEA FROM KASHMIR.` · `WHO COULD BE GREATER THAN YOU?` · `CHANDNI CHOWK, 1675.` · `CHADAR — A SHELTERING CLOTH.` · then, large: `HIND DI CHADAR.`

segments.voice: Think of people anywhere who can't practice their faith freely, or who are pushed to take on one they don't hold; no need to name a country, just let them be people: a family at dinner, a grandmother, a kid at school who hides what she believes. If you pray, pray for their freedom, in your own words or simply with Waheguru. If you don't, wish them room to believe as they choose, and to be left in peace.
Sis Ganj. The gurdwara in Delhi marking where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, after he gave his life so others could keep their faith.
Your line: a shield for others. He covered a faith that wasn't his own. Day one hundred fifty-five.

fork.setup: frightened strangers of another faith ask the Guru for help against forced conversion. what does he do?
options: tell them to join the Sikhs.
go to Delhi himself, and stake his own life on their freedom.

fork.reveal: he sent word that if he could be made to convert, they would all convert, and went to Delhi, where he was executed in 1675.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the covering, or sheltering cloth, of India.

notes: Execution date: commonly 11 November 1675 (observed per the Nanakshahi calendar on 24 November in some years). The script says 'November 1675' and 'late autumn'. Confirm.
The deputation led by Pandit Kirpa Ram, the 'great soul' saying, and the message 'if he converts, we all convert' are tradition. Confirm telling.
Companions Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, Bhai Dayala executed before him: confirm; manner of death omitted deliberately.
Bachittar Natak paraphrase (tilak and janeu; gave his head but not his faith / sees diya par sirar na diya): confirm.
Salok Mahalla 9, 16 (bhai kahu kau det nahi...) at Ang 1427, paraphrased. Confirm Ang and wording of the paraphrase.
Framing: the script names Aurangzeb's officials and avoids any generalization about Muslims. Check tone.
